newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator agrees to change nuclear waste bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator agrees to change nuclear waste bill.

text.p: In a bid to win veto-proof support for a controversial bill, U.S. Senator Frank Murkowski said Monday he had agreed to make "significant changes" in a proposal to store nuclear waste from power plants.
Senators Monday began debating whether to allow the legislation by Alaska Republican Murkowski to come to the floor.

The bill, pushed by nuclear utilities, would require the government to build a temporary storage facility for 30,000 tons of spent fuel from nuclear plants by the end of 1999, which it would need until it has a permanent dump ready.

In a letter to senators, Murkowski said he was prepared to "extend the schedule for siting and licensing an interim facility," one of the key sticking points in the bill which the White House has repeatedly threatened to veto.
"This allows even more time for the progress at the permanent repositoy program at the Yucca Mountain site to be taken into account in siting the interim facility," he said.

Nevada's Yucca Mountain is the only site the Energy Department is investigating as a potential permanent dump for spent nuclear fuel. It expects to make a decision in the fall of 1998 on whether the site would be suitable.

Energy Secretary Federico Pena made clear last week that the administration opposed any move that would force the government to build storage in Nevada before it knows whether Yucca Mountain would be safe for a permanent dump.

Anti-nuclear groups and environmentalists do not want the government to haul the radioactive waste from reactors around the country to a central site until it knows exactly where the waste will be buried permanently.
The administration said Monday it also strongly objected to provisions in the bill that would block the Environmental Protection Agency from setting acceptable radiation release standards.
Murkowski said he would address that problem and "provide that the Environmental Protection Agency will set radiation standards for the permanent repository."
Battling to keep the bill off the Senate floor, Nevada Democrat Sen. Harry Reid warned that the proposed changes in the bill were a sham.
"When the facts come down, you will find that their amendments mean virtually nothing," Reid said in a Senate floor speech.

Under law, the government was supposed to start taking responsibility for the commercial nuclear waste by February 1998, but the Energy Department now expects to have a dump ready only in 2010, at the earliest.

More than 25 nuclear plants expect to start running out of space in their spent fuel cooling pools by February 1998 and do not want to have to pay for building new onsite storage if the government breaks its contract to take over the waste.
